title: A hyperbolic group that is not residually finite
author: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
description: An exposition of OpenAI's proof (2026) that there is a torsion-free word-hyperbolic group that is not residually finite: the fundamental group of a finite complex of Euclidean triangles with three vertices, in which one fixed nonidentity element dies in every finite quotient and is killed by every finite-dimensional linear representation over every field. The first five lessons prove a criterion for complexes whose vertex links have no short closed walks: closed edge paths with large turns are nontrivial, the fundamental group is torsion-free, and it is word-hyperbolic. The first lesson states the theorem and the criterion and proves the metric facts; the second proves the facts on polygons and plane graphs used later (diagonals, cross-cuts, triangulated disks, Euler's formula, models of faces); the third constructs reduced planar fillings of nullhomotopic edge paths through labelled pictures; the fourth proves angular Gauss-Bonnet, the nontriviality of closed paths with large turns and torsion-freeness; the fifth proves uniform thinness of reduced diagrams, a stability lemma for controlled paths and word-hyperbolicity. The sixth lesson constructs random punctured lines over a finite field with no short cycles, the complex and its links, and the rectangular words; the seventh proves that no finite quotient keeps all rectangular words alive, by comparing ranks over the reals and over a fixed prime field, and derives the theorem and, with Malcev's theorem, the corollary on linear representations.
prerequisites: course Constant-coefficient equations and solvability, lesson Polygonal regions and the directions on a circle: the index of a closed polygonal path and its jump across an edge (Lemma 2.1) and the polygonal Jordan separation theorem (Theorem 3.1)

course AG-CA, lesson The Nullstellensatz and Jacobson rings: the integers form a Jacobson ring (Proposition 3.2); finite-type algebras over Jacobson rings are Jacobson with finite residue field extensions (Theorem 4.2); used for Malcev's theorem
core course Algebraic Topology: fundamental groups and homotopy of loops

core course Real Analysis (Lebl, Basic Analysis I): the Lebesgue covering lemma (Lemma 7.4.10), uniform continuity on compact metric spaces (Theorem 7.5.11), compactness and connectedness of metric spaces
linear algebra over fields (ranks, determinants, Gram-Schmidt, tensor products of matrices), finite groups and finite fields

checks.reading: The manuscript 'A torsion-free hyperbolic group that is not residually finite' (OpenAI, 23 Sep 2026; paper.tex of 105 lines and four section files of 7, 296, 431 and 399 lines, fetched at openai/math commit 1581d4cb) was read in full on 14 Oct 2026, and every step of its argument was derived again while the lessons were written: the incidence lemma with its first and second moment estimates, the count of short cycles and the deletion; the blocks and the complex; the links of the three vertices and the same-label distances; the nontriviality of the rectangular words; rank under reduction by Hadamard's inequality and divisibility of a minor; the traces of the arrays of permutation matrices; the local factorization of block sums; sums of polynomials over lines and the line certificate; the tensor identity and the budget; the barycentric subdivision and its links; the intrinsic metric, shortest paths and turns of local geodesics; reduced fillings through labelled pictures, cancellation of node pairs and the dual diagram; angular Gauss-Bonnet, closed paths with large turns and shortest loops; uniform thinness through the Jordan disk of a geodesic polygon, the count of excess vertices, the inradius and the level arc; the stability lemma; the transfer to the Cayley graph and triangles with corners inside edges. No error found. Differences of presentation, none a correction: the facts on polygons and plane graphs (diagonals, cross-cuts, triangulated disks, Euler's formula, models of faces) are proved in the second lesson, with the polygonal Jordan theorem taken from the programme; the cells of a diagram are identified with their models piecewise linearly, so that geodesic polygons are polygons in the plane; the Jordan disk of a geodesic polygon is triangulated without new interior vertices, with a separate case for a polygon inside one triangle; the vertices a and b of the level-arc argument are made vertices of the fine triangulation; the routing to edge paths starts from a polygonal path of nearly minimal length; Markov's and Chebyshev's inequalities, Hadamard's inequality and Malcev's theorem (through Jacobson rings) are proved in the lessons. Checked by the program plan/checks_20261014/rf_check.py (ten parts: block arithmetic for r up to 40; the links of toy complexes over F_13, F_17 and F_23, with the link of O complete bipartite without multiple edges, locally injective projections at V and W, the girth of the link of V at least that of the incidence graph and the same-label distances at least that girth; rank under reduction on 300 random and five structured matrices; traces and ranks of arrays of permutation matrices of S_4 and S_5, also modulo primes dividing the group order; the local factorization of block sums; sums of all monomials of degree below q - 1 over the 182 lines of the plane over F_13 and the line certificate; the tensor identity; the diagonals of Lemma 2.1 of the second lesson and triangulations of 524 random simple polygons, 169 with straight-angle vertices; the law of cosines identity and the constants of the fifth lesson; angular Gauss-Bonnet and the counts on 40 planar diagrams with pendant chains). Run a passed with a smaller polygon sample; run b, with 1,500 polygon draws, passes all ten parts (output rf_check_run_20261014b.txt).
checks.layout: Measured on 14 Oct 2026 in the staged reader at 1100, 768, 543 and 375 px: lessons 1 to 7 have 130, 434, 238, 154, 653, 329 and 305 formulas, 0 rendering errors, 0 wide formulas, no sideways page scroll. After the first measurement 10 formulas were stacked or split (script fix_rfw1.py): the angular Gauss-Bonnet sum, two estimates of the fifth lesson, three displays of the sixth (the Chebyshev bound, the size of a block, the block bijection) and four of the seventh (the trace bound, the factors A_u and B_v, the tensor identity, the rank budget).

open_obligations: The programme results used from other courses are cited with their numbers: the index of a closed polygonal path and the polygonal Jordan theorem (lesson Polygonal regions and the directions on a circle, Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 3.1), and the Jacobson property with finite residue fields (lesson The Nullstellensatz and Jacobson rings, Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 4.2); their statements were compared with the uses, and their proofs were not checked again for this course.

Standard background from the core courses is used without a numbered reference in the lessons: fundamental groups and homotopy of loops, the Lebesgue covering lemma and uniform continuity on compact metric spaces, connectedness and the intermediate value theorem.
The theorem is existential: the course proves that some rectangular word lies in the finite residual, without identifying which one, as does the manuscript.
The lessons were written and checked by one model in one session; they have not been checked by a second reader.
